analysis.one_liner: Caps out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $250 per person per month for insured patients.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to its health committee the day it was introduced and never acted on it, so no drug cost-sharing cap ever came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would limit what people with health insurance pay out of pocket for prescription drugs to $250 a month for an individual, or $500 for a family, starting in 2023, with the cap rising with medical inflation after that. It would apply both to Affordable Care Act marketplace plans and to employer-sponsored group health plans. Instead of facing unlimited drug cost-sharing up to their deductible or out-of-pocket maximum, patients would never pay more than the cap for covered drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 160 million-plus Americans with health coverage through work or through ACA marketplace plans who use prescription drugs — especially anyone with expensive or ongoing prescriptions, who currently can face thousands of dollars in drug cost-sharing before reaching their deductible or out-of-pocket maximum. Under the bill, their monthly drug costs would be capped at $250 per person, no matter the price of the drug [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured people with high drug costs

how_it_helps.text: Caps covered-drug cost-sharing at $250 per person per month ($500 per family) for plan years starting in 2023, so no patient with insurance could be charged more than that in a month for covered prescription drugs.
Applies the cap to both ACA marketplace plans and employer group health plans, so the protection reaches workers with job-based coverage, not just marketplace enrollees.
Indexes the cap to rise each year with the medical care component of the consumer price index, so the protection keeps pace with medical inflation rather than being frozen in dollar terms.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would absorb drug cost-sharing above the cap, either by taking lower patient collections or by raising premiums for everyone in the plan. The bill does not cut drug list prices, so pharmaceutical companies would keep collecting their full prices; the money simply shifts from patients' pockets to premiums and insurer balance sheets [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and all premium payers

drawbacks.text: The bill caps what patients pay but does not lower what drugs cost. Insurers would cover the difference above the cap and would likely raise premiums for everyone in the plan, so many people who rarely fill prescriptions would pay more each month in premiums to protect those who do.

Because drug prices themselves are untouched, pharmaceutical companies keep selling at full price and the bill gives them no new incentive to lower list prices — the affordability problem is masked rather than fixed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients with expensive or chronic prescriptions the cap is a real, immediate relief — no month could cost them more than $250 out of pocket for covered drugs. The trade-off is real too: the bill shifts costs rather than reducing them, so premiums would rise and spread the burden across all enrollees, and drug makers face no new pressure to cut prices. It is a straightforward affordability protection, not a price-control measure, and its main weakness is what it leaves alone.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Warnock and 10 Democratic colleagues introduced the bill in December 2021, amending the Affordable Care Act to cap prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per person per month starting in 2023.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; the committee took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.
The bill never left committee, so it never received a vote in either chamber and expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers are better off, since they never had to absorb drug cost-sharing above the cap or see their plan design rewritten; patients with high drug costs are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers; high-cost patients gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Raphael Warnock
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 8, 2021 to cap prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per person per month.

for.name: 10 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Sens. Klobuchar, Menendez, Baldwin, Reed, Murray, Smith, Heinrich, Blumenthal, Hirono, and Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Patty Murray (D-WA), who was also a cosponsor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on December 8, 2021 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; with no committee action there was nothing to schedule, and no floor vote ever occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican ever cosponsored it, but no vote was ever held, so the actual partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The cap removes their ability to charge patients unlimited drug cost-sharing, shifting that cost onto premiums and insurer margins. Insurer interest in killing the bill ran against patients who would have gained the cap.

The bill leaves drug list prices untouched; cheaper access for patients could even increase prescriptions filled, and the industry bears none of the new cost — that falls on insurers and premium payers.
